Gut microbiota-derived metabolites in aortic diseases

Mechanisms of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in aortic diseases. This illustration summarizes the roles of four major classes of gut-derived metabolites in vascular homeostasis and pathology, within the gut-liver-vascular axis. (a) Trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), derived from choline, L-carnitine, and phosphatidylcholine via trimethylamine (TMA), induces reactive oxygen species (ROS), endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (via PERK-ATF4/5-CHOP), and vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) apoptosis. (b) Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), like butyrate and propionate, acting through receptors such as GPR41/43 and histone deacetylases (HDACs), reduce ROS, promote Treg differentiation from naive T cells, inhibit NLRP3/NFκB in M1 macrophages, and support a synthetic VSMC phenotype. (c) Secondary bile acids, including ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), modulate FXR-CRE2 signaling to decrease ceramide, MMP2/9, and VSMC apoptosis, while inhibiting VSMC apoptosis and ROS via NRF2 and palmitate-serine pathways. (d) Tryptophan metabolism: Under pathological conditions, tryptophan metabolism shifts from the protective gut microbiota-mediated indole pathway to the host-driven kynurenine pathway, contributing to extracellular matrix degradation and disease progression in aneurysms, dissections, and atherosclerosis.
